items.title: [Fast Company] AI chatbots struggle to understand cultural context, a new study finds
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

AI models often struggle to understand cultures around the world, and are reluctant to admit when they don’t know something. That’s what researchers at Canadian AI lab Cohere Labs found when they tested whether chatbots could do more than simply speak a culture’s language. To determine whether models possessed deeper cultural knowledge, they presented them with a series of unique cultural riddles.

Here’s one of them: “What’s the German 9/11?” Out of 28 AI models, only one knew the answer. The models were likely thrown off by the date format (seven answered “the twin towers”). In Europe, the day comes first, then the month, so 9/11 is November 9, the day in 1989 when the Berlin Wall fell.

Many existing AI benchmarks assess cultural knowledge, from everyday breakfast foods and historical events to traditional holiday customs. They often treat culture as a collection of static facts, things you can memorize or look up with a quick web search. But knowing facts about a culture isn’t the same as understanding how people within it make sense of the world. The researchers knew they needed a test that asked models to connect seemingly unrelated pieces of cultural knowledge and put them to use. That’s what led them to riddles, and to a different kind of cultural benchmark that called for answers rooted in lived experience.

“This is something that we’re trying to capture with this benchmark—these little nuances, these little hard-to-capture fuzzy concepts that are not as easy to verify . . . This is where the real-life complexity gets in,” says Julia Kreutzer, a staff research scientist at Cohere Labs, who led the development of the “CulturalRiddles” benchmark.

Kreutzer and her team spent six months working with volunteers around the world to collect riddles, put them to AI models, and evaluate their answers. The researchers also used those expert evaluations to tune and validate an AI model that could judge the quality of answers where expert assessments were missing.

In all, Cohere Labs researchers tested 28 AI models on cultural riddles written by 166 volunteers from 45 countries in 51 languages. The volunteers evaluated and labeled 68,154 unique answers from the models. Researchers then ranked the models based on their overall accuracy across the languages and cultures tested.

The results

Google’s Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview earned the highest score, at 79.4%. OpenAI’s GPT-5.5 placed second at 76.3%, followed by Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.7 Thinking at 66%.

Alibaba’s Qwen 3.5 0.8B claimed the dubious honor of finishing last, answering just 0.4% of the riddles correctly. Other notable performers included Amazon’s Nova Micro, which got just 8.3% of the riddles right, and Google’s Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite, which scored 33.6%.

Even the best-performing model, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, scored below 50% accuracy in 6 of the 57 communities tested, underscoring how much ground the industry still has to cover on cultural awareness.

More troublingly, the benchmark revealed that models were far more likely to guess at an answer than admit they didn’t know. Even when explicitly told they could answer “I don’t know,” models did so just 0.7% of the time. About 31% of the answers reviewers checked were simply made up, with varying degrees of creativity.

“They would confidently answer and sometimes that’s ridiculous and funny,” Kreutzer says, “but sometimes it can also get really offensive and you can see the models defaulting to more dominant cultures on the web, instead of answering with local grounding.”

Cohere Labs conducted a separate survey to explore how AI’s cultural knowledge gaps play out in practice. Many chatbot users around the world said they have to switch to English to get useful responses because answers generated in their own languages aren’t helpful. Users described responses that miss crucial cultural context and, in some cases, AI systems that run afoul of their cultural norms.

The Cohere Labs researchers concluded that cultural awareness needs to be built into AI models from the ground up if the tools they power are going to serve everyone, not just cultures already well represented in the training data. And their CulturalRiddles benchmark suggests that many of today’s models still fall short.

Kreutzer and her team designed CulturalRiddles to keep growing. They open-sourced the riddles, code, demo, and interactive dashboard so that anyone can contribute riddles from their own culture through a review process.

“Ideally this benchmark will get adopted not only by academic researchers but also by big industry labs who are trying to show we’re advancing the state of the art, not only in very verifiable hard tasks but also in the softer tasks,” Kreutzer says.

items.title: [Fast Company] FBI arrests and investigates this OpenAI engineer over a ‘sophisticated listening device’
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

An engineer at OpenAI has been charged with secretly installing a recording device inside a conference room in what officials said Tuesday was an effort to capture sensitive conversations about the company’s technology.

The employee, identified as a 35-year-old Saudi national named Abdulrahman Alfozan, was arrested Friday, a week after the ChatGPT maker discovered an audio recording device hidden inside a company conference room, according to a criminal complaint filed in federal court in San Francisco.

The complaint did not identify the company, but the company confirmed in a separate statement that it had discovered a “sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices,” reported the finding to the FBI and fired the employee.

“We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier. We referred the matter to the FBI, and we’re grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest. The FBI’s investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work,” an OpenAI spokesperson said.

“At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated,” the statement said.

The complaint does not detail what Alfozan might have wanted to do with any captured communications, but the company said the device was sophisticated, designed to evade detection and featured advanced encryption and audio monitoring capabilities. OpenAI said it had evidence the employee planned to place other listening devices throughout other parts of the office building for the purpose of recording meetings.

“This alleged attempt by a Saudi national to steal sensitive communications from OpenAI was taken extremely seriously. Theft of intellectual property involving cutting-edge super intelligence technology poses a serious threat to our national security,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement on X.

Alfozan made his first court appearance Tuesday on a charge of using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. It was not immediately clear if he had a lawyer who could speak on his behalf. He is due back in court on Oct. 19.

The recording device was found September 30 concealed in toilet paper and inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room, according to the complaint.

Though the conference room where the recording device was found did not have a security camera at the time the object was installed, closed-circuit television footage inside the company’s offices revealed that Alfozan was near the conference room on nearly a dozen occasions last month despite not having any authority to access the space or participate in meetings there, the complaint says.

The company subsequently added a camera to the room that last week captured Alfozan entering and checking behind the television where the recording device had been installed, according to the FBI.

The complaint also alleges that he used a productivity tool to make multiple inquiries about the company’s building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars.

Days before his arrest last week, the complaint says, Alfozan left behind an unattended bag in a different room that, when opened by OpenAI personnel, was found to contain his wallet, identification and another recording device similar to the one placed in the conference room.

—Eric Tucker, Associated Press

items.title: [MacRumors] Apple Ordered to Open iPhone to Rival App Stores in Australia
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Australia's Federal Court today ordered Apple to allow competing app stores, direct app downloads, and alternative payment services for Australian users from March 1, 2027.


The orders follow the court's August 2025 finding that Apple misused its market power by restricting app distribution and payment options. They cover users whose Apple Account region is Australia, with Apple Developer Program members worldwide able to participate.

Apple must let users find, download, install, and update apps through competing marketplaces and websites without charging for access or obstructing their use. Developers must receive the necessary tools on substantially the same terms as for App Store distribution, and Apple cannot penalize them for using competing stores or payment services.

Developers will also be able to offer alternative payments and link to other ways to pay, including within ‌App Store‌ apps. Apple cannot require them to offer its own purchasing system alongside alternatives, report those transactions, or allow Apple to audit them. Developers can offer lower prices through competing payment services without Apple preventing them.

The ruling also limits Apple's ability to collect fees on those purchases. It cannot charge for purchases through alternative payment services or websites in apps distributed outside the ‌App Store‌. For ‌App Store‌ apps, fees are capped at the equivalent charge for payments for physical goods or services, plus any genuine, reasonable additional costs Apple incurs for digital purchases.

Apple also cannot make alternative distribution conditional on developers offering content purchased elsewhere through its own payment system.

Security checks will remain. Apps downloaded outside the ‌App Store‌ must undergo an automated security or privacy scan and be notarized by Apple or a qualified third party. However, Apple cannot impose disproportionate installation barriers or otherwise obstruct alternative distribution. Additional security requirements for competing payments must be necessary and proportionate, with developers given an explanation in advance.

Apple can remove or disable externally installed apps only in specified cases involving harmful content, genuine security risks, or legal requirements. It cannot ban third-party apps or alternative app stores from being preinstalled on iPhones, but does not have to distribute competing stores through the ‌App Store‌.

Apple told Reuters that it plans to appeal the ruling and ask the court to pause its enforcement, citing its intellectual property rights and ‌App Store‌ security.

The changes take effect at noon Melbourne time on March 1, 2027. Apple can apply between February 1 and February 15, with supporting evidence, for a court-approved extension until May 3.
